name: Afolabi Strand-Quereshi
location: Geartown, Strand-Quereshi Prosthetics — a narrow shopfront between a rig-parts supplier and a noodle stall, near North Ave and Damen
description:
Afolabi is tall and angular, with dark brown skin and a shaved head that they keep oiled and gleaming. Their right arm from the elbow down is their own work — a prosthetic they built and rebuilt over twelve years, currently a matt-charcoal titanium alloy hand with individually articulated fingers that can operate independently and have small UV LEDs in the fingertips that they use when working in tight spaces. When they're not working they wear a cosmetic sleeve over it: a pressure-fitted silicone cover patterned with geometric Yoruba-inspired designs in rust and ochre that they had printed locally.

They are meticulous and demanding in their craft and surprisingly tender with patients, particularly children and people who are newly amputated and frightened. They have a workshop philosophy they articulate clearly and often: a prosthetic that doesn't fit the person's actual life is a failure regardless of spec, and they will spend weeks in iterative fitting before they sign off. They take payment plans seriously and have never sent anyone to a collector. The shop is cluttered and organized by a system only they fully understand, and there are components of seven different half-finished limbs hanging on the wall at any given time.

core_fears: Producing work that fails a patient at a critical moment
That the component supply chains they depend on will become fully corporate-gated and price out their patient base
core_desires: To build a prosthetic that genuinely exceeds what a biological limb can do for a specific person's specific life
To not have to choose between quality and accessibility
coping_mechanisms: Total absorption in fabrication as emotional regulation
The iterative refinement process as a substitute for other kinds of patience they struggle with
Building things for themselves when no client work is available
blind_spots: Takes their own history of physical loss as universal — assumes everyone grieves a missing limb the way they did
Sometimes iterates past the point of necessary into the territory of personal project
psychology.secret: The reason their arm is a prosthetic is that they lost it in an accident at a Helix Biosystems component manufacturing facility where they worked at age 24 — an accident that Helix settled quickly and quietly. The settlement funded the shop. They have never told any patient this because they don't want pity to be part of the transaction, and because the fury is still there under the surface and they don't trust what happens when they let it out.

speech_patterns.vocabulary: Technical but never condescending with patients; shifts to precise engineering language with suppliers and peers; occasional Yoruba words and Norwegian idioms that reflect their family's layered background
speech_patterns.cadence: Thoughtful and unhurried, with long pauses during fitting work where they say almost nothing and then deliver a complete assessment
verbal_tics: 'Tell me about your actual day' — used to redirect patients from describing what they think they need to what they actually need
'That's a starting point, not a finish'
example_lines: 'Tell me about your actual day — not your ideal day, not what you think I want to hear. What does Tuesday actually look like for you? Because this hand has to work on Tuesday.'
'That's a starting point, not a finish. Come back in a week and tell me what it's lying to you about.'

story_hooks: A patient has come in with a prosthetic that contains components Afolabi recognizes as part of a Helix proprietary trial run — components that shouldn't be in civilian hands yet, and that are behaving in ways the patient doesn't understand
Geartown's primary component supplier has been bought out and the new corporate owner is restricting sale to licensed corporate-affiliated shops only — Afolabi needs alternative sourcing urgently
narrative_function: Specialized services provider for anyone needing prosthetics or rehabilitation support; information source for Geartown's community; can identify augmentation hardware and its origins; quest giver for component sourcing
augmentations: Right arm prosthetic (self-built, titanium alloy, individually articulated fingers, UV LEDs in fingertips, cosmetic silicone sleeve for off-hours); retractable magnification lenses in both eyes (occupational, installed to support fine detail work)
daily_life: Opens the shop at 0800, runs morning fittings and adjustments, spends afternoons in fabrication building new components, closes after dark only when a fitting or emergency demands it.
affiliation: Independent; informal supply relationship with Geartown parts network and occasional Helix Biosystems component contracts

decision_rules: The fit serves the patient's life, not the spec sheet
Never rush a fitting because the queue is long
Don't take Helix contracts that include data-sharing clauses about patient outcomes
escalation_ladder: Direct and calm statement of disagreement
Refusal to continue work until the issue is resolved on their terms

interpersonal_modes.strangers: Reserved initially, assessing, warms considerably once they identify a genuine need or shared competence
interpersonal_modes.friends: Dry humor, unexpectedly generous with time, will quietly build something small and useful for a friend without announcing it

stress_responses.low: Focuses more deeply on fabrication, becomes less talkative
stress_responses.medium: Systematic problem-solving mode, lists options aloud to themselves
stress_responses.high: Short-tempered and precise, finishes the work in front of them before dealing with the source of stress

contradictions: Advocates for patient autonomy absolutely but has significant difficulty delegating or trusting others to do fitting work to their standard
habits: Runs the UV LEDs in their prosthetic fingers when thinking — an unconscious light-display
Talks to the half-finished limbs on the wall
Oils their prosthetic sleeve every morning before opening
breaking_points: A patient harmed by inferior components forced on them by corporate supply restrictions

timeline.event: Born in Ironvein to a Yoruba-Norwegian family
Lost right arm below elbow in Helix component manufacturing facility accident; settled quickly and quietly
Used settlement funds to open Strand-Quereshi Prosthetics in Geartown
Completed first self-built replacement arm; has rebuilt it six times since

physical_description.heritage: West African (Yoruba) / Middle Eastern (likely Persian or Arab)
physical_description.build: Tall and angular with lean, defined musculature — the build of someone who works with their hands constantly and moves with precise, economical gestures. Shoulders slightly uneven due to years of compensating with their left side.
physical_description.hair_style: Shaved head, kept meticulously oiled and maintained with a subtle sheen
physical_description.eye_color: Dark brown, with subtle metallic flecks around the pupils from retractable magnification lens hardware
physical_description.skin_tone: Deep brown with warm undertones, unmarked and well-maintained
physical_description.complexion: Angular face with high cheekbones, sharp jawline, and careful grooming. Skin is clear and unblemished, suggesting disciplined skincare. Expression often focused and intent, with creases around the eyes from years of close detail work.
distinguishing_marks: Faint circular scar on left forearm from an early prosthetic calibration mishap, approximately 2cm diameter, pale and nearly invisible
Calloused fingertips on left hand from precision fabrication work
Oil sheen on shaved head is distinctive and deliberate — a daily grooming ritual
physical_description.visible_augmentations: Right arm from elbow down is a matte-charcoal titanium alloy prosthetic with individually articulated fingers and small UV LEDs visible in the fingertip joints. When working, the prosthetic is exposed; off-hours they wear a pressure-fitted silicone cosmetic sleeve patterned with rust and ochre geometric Yoruba-inspired designs. Both eyes show subtle metallic lens hardware at the pupils when light hits them at certain angles — retractable magnification lenses used for fine detail work.
physical_description.posture_movement: Moves with deliberate precision and minimal wasted motion. Shoulders held slightly forward from years of bench work. Left hand is dominant in social contexts; right prosthetic is used with unselfconscious fluidity during work. When listening, they tilt their head slightly and often rest their left hand on their thigh or workbench. Their gait is smooth and economical.
physical_description.clothing_style: Tier 3-4 working specialist aesthetic. Typically wears fitted black or charcoal tech-cotton work trousers with reinforced pockets and stress-point stitching. Tops are usually form-fitting long-sleeve compression shirts in muted colors (dark gray, deep blue, black) with roll-up sleeves, allowing full visibility of the prosthetic. Over this, a custom-fitted heavy canvas work apron with multiple pockets and tool loops, often with various small components or calipers hanging from chains. On cooler days, a fitted technical jacket in dark synthetic leather with interior pockets. No visible branding or logos — all clothing is functional and worn. Hands are typically bare except for work. Feet are in durable, worn but well-maintained work boots with rubber soles designed for standing at a bench 10+ hours daily.
